tagline: A river with a country wrapped around it
overview:
The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a thin strip of land following the Gambia River for about 450 kilometers inland from the Atlantic Ocean. Never more than 50 kilometers wide, it is surrounded on three sides by Senegal, like a finger poking into its neighbor. The whole country is smaller than Connecticut. The capital, Banjul, sits on an island at the river's mouth, though most people live in the nearby fast-growing coastal towns around Serekunda.

About 2.7 million people live in The Gambia, making it densely populated for Africa. English is the official language, and Mandinka, Wolof, and Fula are the most widely spoken at home. Most Gambians are Muslim. The country is a republic that returned to democracy in 2017 after 22 years under a strongman president. Farmers grow peanuts, rice, and millet along the river, fishermen bring in catches from the Atlantic, and tourists come to the beaches, especially from Europe in winter, for sun and birdwatching. Gambians call their country the Smiling Coast of Africa.
landAndNature: The Gambia River is everything here. It flows wide and salty between mangrove swamps near the coast, where oysters cling to roots, and becomes a fresh, winding ribbon between low sandstone banks upstream. The land on either side is flat savanna of grasses, baobabs, and palms, rarely rising more than 50 meters. Hippos and crocodiles live in the river's middle stretches, and chimpanzees rehabilitated on the Baboon Islands in the River Gambia National Park have formed thriving troops. The country is a birdwatcher's paradise, with more than 500 species recorded in a tiny area, from kingfishers and bee-eaters to fish eagles. The climate is hot, with a rainy season from June to October and dry, dusty months in between.
peopleAndCulture: Gambians belong mainly to the Mandinka, Fula, Wolof, Jola, and Serahule peoples, who live peacefully together and often speak several languages. Meals center on rice: benachin is a one-pot dish of rice, fish or meat, and vegetables, and domoda is a rich peanut stew. Attaya, strong green tea poured in three rounds, is shared for hours. Music comes from the kora, a 21-string harp made from a large gourd, played by griots, hereditary musicians who keep family histories in song. Wrestling matches with drumming and dancing draw big crowds, and soccer is the favorite sport. Gambian women make colorful tie-dyed cloth, and naming ceremonies and weddings are celebrated with feasts for the whole neighborhood.
history: Stone circles at Wassu and Kerbatch, some 1,200 years old, show that organized societies lived along the river long ago. The area later formed part of the Mali and Songhai empires and Mandinka kingdoms. Portuguese explorers arrived in the 1450s, and from the 1600s British and French traders competed here, shipping many thousands of enslaved people from posts such as James Island, now Kunta Kinteh Island, whose name honors the ancestor of the writer Alex Haley. Britain made the river a colony in 1888. The Gambia became independent on February 18, 1965, under Dawda Jawara, and was a democracy until Yahya Jammeh seized power in 1994 and ruled harshly for 22 years. He refused to accept an election defeat in 2016 but was forced out by neighboring countries in 2017.
funFacts: The Gambia is one of very few countries whose name officially includes The, a rule set when it became independent.
At its narrowest the country is only about 24 kilometers wide, and Senegal surrounds it on three sides.
Kunta Kinteh Island, a former slave-trading fort, is named after the ancestor in Alex Haley's book Roots.
More than 500 bird species have been recorded in The Gambia, an area smaller than Connecticut.
The Wassu stone circles are made of laterite pillars up to two meters tall, raised more than a thousand years ago.
